blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a paper that explores the risks of smart contracts being used for criminal activities, termed 'criminal smart contracts' (CSCs). The authors demonstrate how CSCs could facilitate crimes like information leakage, theft of cryptographic keys, and even physical crimes (e.g., murder, arson). A key concept introduced is 'commission-fairness,' ensuring that either both the crime and payment occur, or neither does. The paper also discusses the advantages of decentralized smart contracts for criminals, such as enabling fair exchange without intermediaries and minimizing interaction to evade law enforcement. Colyer notes that while the paper focuses on preventing misuse, the proposed techniques could also benefit legitimate contracts. The blog post delves into specific scenarios like incentivized information leakage and buying stolen private keys, illustrating the technical challenges and cryptographic solutions involved.
paper_title: The Ring of Gyges: investigating the future of criminal smart contracts
paper_abstract: My work that was recognized by the 2015 ACM Turing Award is in cybersecurity, while my primary interest for the last 35 years has been international security with an emphasis on reducing the risk that nuclear deterrence will fail and destroy civilization. This ACM Turing Lecture draws connections between those seemingly disparate areas and Alan Turing’s elegant proof that the computable real numbers, while denumerable, are not effectively denumerable. Martin E. Hellman is best known for his invention, with Diffie and Merkle, of public key cryptography, the technology that, among other uses, enables secure Internet transactions. It is used to transfer literally trillions of dollars every day. He has been a long-time contributor to the computer privacy debate, and was a key participant in the “first crypto war” of the late 1970s and early 80s that established the right of academic cryptographic researchers to publish their papers, free of government interference. His work has been recognized by a number of honors and awards, including election to the National Academy of Engineering, induction as one of the first two dozen “Stanford Engineering Heroes,” the National Inventors Hall of Fame, and the Marconi International Fellowship – and, keynotes Ross Anderson University of Cambridge, UK Is it practical to build a truly distributed payment system? most recently, the 2015 ACM Turing Award, often called “the Nobel Prize of Computer Science.” More detailed information is available on his honors and awards, his university service, and his professional and civic service. Hellman has a deep interest in the ethics of technological development, and one of his current activities is applying risk analysis to a potential failure of nuclear deterrence. That approach has been endorsed by a number of prominent individuals including former Director of the National Security Agency (NSA) Adm. Bobby Inman and Stanford’s President Emeritus Donald Kennedy.
